---
title: "Variable and value labels"
---

Parquet holds values, not labels. ggp-client keeps the labels of every `.dta` and `.sav` file, as pyreadstat reads
them, in a `meta.json` next to its parquet file. Variable names are lower case, in the parquet files and in their
`meta.json` (`DEM01` in a download is `dem01`); the raw downloads keep the portal's names.

## Putting the labels on the data

```python
from ggp_client import labels, read

path = "data/download/consolidated/ggs-ii_w1.parquet"
meta = labels.meta(path)                  # the meta.json next to it
df = labels.label(read.read(path), meta)  # every labelled column holds its labels: 1 -> "Male"
labels.variable_labels(df, meta)          # {"dem01": "Gender", ...}
```

`labels.label` turns each column with value labels into a categorical column (a polars `Enum`, or a pandas
`Categorical` for a pandas frame), with the labels in the order of their codes. A code without a label shows as itself
(`"7"`), and missing stays missing. `columns=["dem01"]` labels only those. A pandas frame also gets the variable
labels, in `df.attrs["column_labels"]`. `labels.meta` also reads the labels of a `.dta` or `.sav` file.

## The labels themselves

```python
meta["column_labels"]["dem01"]   # 'Gender'                                    variable -> variable label
meta["value_labels"]["dem01"]    # {'1': 'Male', '2': 'Female', '3': 'Other', ...}  variable -> value -> label
```

JSON keys are text, so codes are `"1"`, not `1`. To hand labels back to pyreadstat:

```python
import pyreadstat

labels = {int(k): v for k, v in meta["value_labels"]["dem01"].items() if k.lstrip("-").isdigit()}
pyreadstat.write_dta(df.select("dem01"), "gender.dta", variable_value_labels={"dem01": labels},
                     column_labels=[meta["column_labels"]["dem01"]])
```

Letter codes such as `"b"` are Stata's extended missing values (`.b`); pyreadstat reads those cells as missing.

## Per-file meta.json

| key | content |
|---|---|
| `file` | the source file, under `download/raw` |
| `file_label` | the file's own label |
| `column_labels` | `{variable: label}` |
| `value_labels` | `{variable: {value: label}}` |
| `missing_ranges` | `.sav` only: the values SPSS treats as missing |
| `original_types` | the Stata or SPSS display format of each variable |

## Consolidated meta.json: harmonized labels

Countries label the same variable and the same values differently: "Czechia" or "Czech Republic", or `region` 1
meaning "East Austria" in one country and "East Midlands" in another. The consolidated `meta.json` has one
harmonized set:

- **One vote per country**, that of its first file (Belarus ships GGS-II wave 1 in English and in Russian; the
  English file votes). Harmonized Histories and Additional Datasets, which have no country, vote per file.
- **Every variable has one label**: the one most countries use (`respid`: "Respondent ID").
- **Every value has exactly one label**: the one more than half of the countries use (ISO 203: "Czechia"). With
  no majority, all labels are joined into one, most used first (`region` 1: "East Austria / East Midlands /
  Pannonian Croatia / ..."). Spelling and case variants count as the same label.
- **Several values may share a label**: `dem07` 2102 (Austria) and 3103 (Croatia) are both "Elementary school".
- **Codes are never changed**: the data is exactly what each country delivered.
- **`original_labels`** lists, for every value labelled differently in any file, each wording and the files
  that use it:

```json
"intdatem": {"c": {"Don't know": ["ggs-ii/w1/by/.../GGP2020_WAVE1_BLR_V_1_0.dta", "..."],
                   "Не знаю": ["ggs-ii/w1/by/.../GGP2020_WAVE1_BLR_V_1_0_RU.dta"]}}
```

The labelled Stata files written by `download_ggs.py` (`consolidate.to_stata`) use these same labels. Stata
attaches value labels to whole numbers only, so they go on integer columns and on decimal columns that hold only
whole numbers.
